canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is an image-question task: models receive visual input, most often a single image, plus a natural-language question, and are expected to produce a textual answer based on the visual content. Several definitions make the image-question pair explicit and describe the task as requiring joint use of image and text inputs, while some papers specify short answers or autoregressive answers. A smaller line of work broadens the visual source to one or more images, 3D scenes, videos, webpages or website screenshots, embedded images, generated images, or medical images, and one paper asks for both an answer and an explanation.

Variants. Most variants stay close to general image question answering, sometimes split into single-image QA, simple QA, text-related VQA, or image-agnostic versus image-specific prompts. Smaller strands study 3D visual question answering, region-text interleaved VQA, GUI question answering, embedded image question answering, and scene text question answering. Other papers specialize the same pattern to medical, object-focused, region-focused, or algorithmic-puzzle settings.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 45 measurement instruments, with VQA-v2, GQA, VizWiz, TextVQA, and OK-VQA appearing most often. Elicitation is usually an image plus question, sometimes with a short-answer prompt, but several papers use multiple-choice formats with one ground-truth answer, standard four-option questions, or yes/no object-presence questions. Scoring is commonly reported as benchmark accuracy, and one paper uses a pretrained LLM to check whether a prediction is semantically equivalent to the ground truth; other instruments span science- and knowledge-oriented VQA, medical and document VQA, region-focused evaluation, and video QA.

What it is taken as evidence of. The prevailing usage treats visual question answering as evidence of multimodal understanding and visual perception: papers describe it as a multimodal understanding task, use image or image/video question answering to measure multimodal understanding, and in one case use VQA accuracy as a proxy for perception capability. Papers link it to 15 constructs overall; after those two, the most frequent links are to visual grounding and visual understanding, usually as related constructs, though individual papers claim causal relationships from visual grounding to improved VQA performance and from visual understanding to the ability to handle VQA tasks. Another paper claims a causal relationship from visual question-answering instructions to brain alignment, so the papers do not converge on a single construct that this behavior reflects.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across the papers, the dominant framing is an image-question task: models receive visual input, most often a single image, plus a natural-language question, and are expected to produce a textual answer based on the visual content. Several definitions make the image-question pair explicit and describe the task as requiring joint use of image and text inputs, while some papers specify short answers or autoregressive answers. A smaller line of work broadens the visual source to one or more images, 3D scenes, videos, webpages or website screenshots, embedded images, generated images, or medical images, and one paper asks for both an answer and an explanation.

characterization_sections.label: Variants.
characterization_sections.text: Most variants stay close to general image question answering, sometimes split into single-image QA, simple QA, text-related VQA, or image-agnostic versus image-specific prompts. Smaller strands study 3D visual question answering, region-text interleaved VQA, GUI question answering, embedded image question answering, and scene text question answering. Other papers specialize the same pattern to medical, object-focused, region-focused, or algorithmic-puzzle settings.

characterization_sections.label: Space of elicitation and scores.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link this behavior to 45 measurement instruments, with VQA-v2, GQA, VizWiz, TextVQA, and OK-VQA appearing most often. Elicitation is usually an image plus question, sometimes with a short-answer prompt, but several papers use multiple-choice formats with one ground-truth answer, standard four-option questions, or yes/no object-presence questions. Scoring is commonly reported as benchmark accuracy, and one paper uses a pretrained LLM to check whether a prediction is semantically equivalent to the ground truth; other instruments span science- and knowledge-oriented VQA, medical and document VQA, region-focused evaluation, and video QA.

characterization_sections.label: What it is taken as evidence of.
characterization_sections.text: The prevailing usage treats visual question answering as evidence of multimodal understanding and visual perception: papers describe it as a multimodal understanding task, use image or image/video question answering to measure multimodal understanding, and in one case use VQA accuracy as a proxy for perception capability. Papers link it to 15 constructs overall; after those two, the most frequent links are to visual grounding and visual understanding, usually as related constructs, though individual papers claim causal relationships from visual grounding to improved VQA performance and from visual understanding to the ability to handle VQA tasks. Another paper claims a causal relationship from visual question-answering instructions to brain alignment, so the papers do not converge on a single construct that this behavior reflects.
